result.owner_input_fidelity_observation: Comfort typing feels clunky and less fluid than the native REPL; physical key presses are frequently not registered and must be repeated.
result.classification: FIRST RED: loss of ordinary physical input is a correctness failure, not a cosmetic latency finding

host_attribution.hardware_overflow_rule: a sixth event is not enqueued while the five-event queue is full
host_attribution.comfort_input_path: key-event allocates a three-cell (key code modifiers) tuple; an accepted printable allocates one editor cell; synchronous edit/render work completes before the next queue poll
host_attribution.native_repl_control: lisp_input_event writes one event to a stack struct and the native REPL appends the code directly to its static C buffer before polling again
host_attribution.mechanism_class: the synchronous Lisp consumer has service gaps larger than the finite producer queue can absorb; periodic collection is the strongest pre-registered gap term, while the exact current screen/VM/GC split remains unmeasured
host_attribution.gate_gap: the accepted allocation gate bounded one collection per key but never related that pause to the five-event queue or asserted zero dropped physical input

next.device_contacts: closed until a host-priced input-fidelity repair exists
next.required_property: ordinary physical keys cannot be lost while editor work or collection is in progress
pricing_candidates: capture into a product-owned queue independently of Lisp edit/render/GC work
a zero-allocation scalar event path plus preallocated editor storage, with an explicit queue-service bound
queue-aware drain/coalescing only if its event materialization cannot itself collect before the hardware queue is drained

claim_limit.reason: The same-world delta proves the listed semantics, but the owner's physical typing observation is a release-relevant input-fidelity First Red. No exact current GC timing or individual dropped-key count is claimed.
